name: Bloomreach
tagline: Enterprise commerce suite: AI product search and merchandising, plus a customer data platform with cross-channel campaign automation.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Bloomreach sells enterprise contracts quoted per catalog size, traffic and module mix, with no public price list.

verdictSummary: Bloomreach is two heavy products bolted together: a product discovery engine that ranks a large catalog using live clickstream and conversion signals, and a CDP that stitches identities and fires email, SMS and on-site campaigns off those events. You can absolutely build semantic product search over your own catalog in an afternoon, and it will feel good on a thousand SKUs. What you cannot one-shot is the part that actually earns the contract: ingesting millions of events a day, keeping identity graphs coherent, letting merchandisers tune ranking without a deploy, and sending campaign volume that lands in inboxes. This is also a product bought by committees that need SLAs, SOC 2, data processing agreements and someone to call at 2am. A personal replacement is not a thing, because there is no personal version of this problem.
coreLoopDIY: Index your own product catalog with embeddings plus keyword search, log clicks, and re-rank results using the click data you collected.
requirements: A product catalog you control, as CSV or JSON
An embeddings API key in .env, or a local embedding model
Real traffic, otherwise the click-based re-ranking has nothing to learn from
Your own storefront to wire the search endpoint into
whatYouLose: Real-time identity stitching across web, email, app and offline, which is most of what a CDP is
Campaign sending at volume, with deliverability, suppression lists and consent tracking handled for you
Merchandiser-facing tooling: ranking rules, pinning, banners, A/B tests, all without engineering
Pretrained relevance from years of retail clickstream, so your cold-start ranking is just vector similarity
SOC 2, GDPR tooling, DPAs, uptime SLAs and a support line, which is why procurement signed in the first place
moatNotes: The ranking models are fed by aggregate shopper behavior across many retailers. A single store cannot reproduce that signal, no matter how good the code is.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the buyer is a retailer with a hundred thousand SKUs and a merchandising team, not a developer with a weekend. They pay for search that converts on day one rather than after six months of click data, for a marketing team that can launch a segmented campaign without filing a ticket, and for a vendor that signs a DPA and answers the phone when checkout search goes down on Black Friday. The code is the cheap part. The operational guarantees and the behavioral data are the product.
notes: Semantic search over your own catalog is genuinely a weekend build, and worth doing. The moat is aggregate retail clickstream plus the enterprise paperwork that lets a 500-store chain route live checkout traffic through someone else's ranker.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted product discovery service for a single store catalog. Consolation build for Bloomreach Discovery, not a clone.

Stack, no substitutions: TypeScript, Node 20, Express, SQLite via better-sqlite3 with the FTS5 extension, and sqlite-vec for vector search. Server-rendered HTML with plain templates and a little vanilla JS. No React, no framework, no cloud services beyond one embeddings API.

What to build:
1. `npm run ingest -- catalog.csv` reads a CSV with columns id, title, description, category, brand, price, image_url, in_stock. Upsert into a `products` table.
2. During ingest, embed `title + brand + category + description` using the OpenAI embeddings API, key read from OPENAI_API_KEY in .env. Batch requests, cache by content hash so re-ingest is cheap, store vectors in sqlite-vec.
3. Also index title, brand, category and description into an FTS5 table.
4. GET /search?q=&session= runs both: FTS5 BM25 and vector nearest neighbors. Fuse with reciprocal rank fusion. Filter out of stock items to the bottom, never hide them. Return JSON.
5. Faceting: return counts by category, brand and three price buckets for the current result set. Support &category=, &brand=, &price_min=, &price_max=.
6. Event logging: POST /events with {session, query, product_id, type} where type is impression, click or add_to_cart. Store in an `events` table with timestamps.
7. Re-ranking: a `npm run rerank` script computes, per query token and product, a click-through score from the events table and writes it to a `boosts` table. Search applies boosts as a multiplier, capped so a popular item cannot bury an exact title match.
8. A `synonyms.json` file expands query terms before FTS5. Hand-edited, loaded at boot.
9. A minimal /admin page: search box, live results, and the ability to pin a product id to the top for a given query, persisted in a `pins` table.
10. A demo storefront at / with a search bar and a result grid that fires impression and click events.

Explicitly out of scope: multi-tenancy, user accounts, auth on /admin beyond a shared ADMIN_TOKEN in .env, A/B testing, email, SMS, identity stitching, recommendations widgets, and any analytics dashboard beyond a /stats page printing top queries and zero-result queries.

Ship a seed script that generates 200 fake products so it runs with no catalog. README: setup, .env keys, ingest, rerank cron suggestion, and a blunt note that click-based re-ranking does nothing until there is real traffic.
